content:
The discovery offers a rare look at how giant stellar pairs live and die over thousands of years. By analyzing how both explosions shaped the surrounding environment, scientists can reconstruct the full lifecycle of a binary system from birth to ultimate collapse.

How two distant clouds share one hydrogen cloud

Lead author Miltiadis Michailidis of Stanford University worked alongside an international team to study the two wreckage sites, known as IC 443 and G189.6+3.3. While IC 443 is widely known as the Jellyfish Nebula, G189.6+3.3 forms a nearby fainter ring of gas.

The team combined sixteen years of gamma-ray data from NASA’s Fermi Space Telescope with detailed radio, X-ray, and optical images. Their analysis proved that both expanding gas shells are slamming into the same interstellar cloud of hydrogen.

Because both remnants interact with the same cloud, they must sit at the same distance from Earth, about 6,000 light-years away. Their explosion centers lie 30 to 50 light-years apart within the same region of space.

Statistical modeling showed that two unrelated stars randomly exploding so close together was virtually impossible. So, the team concluded that both stars formed together from the same parent cloud before expanding outward.

Two explosions separated by tens of thousands of years

Although the two stars belonged to the same original system, they did not end their lives at the same time. The team estimates that the star behind G189.6+3.3 exploded between 20,000 and 100,000 years before its companion star detonated.

Both original stars were massive giants, each weighing more than ten times as much as our Sun. The star that created IC 443 held an estimated 15 to 25 times the mass of the Sun, while its partner held at least 20.

When stars that large exhaust their fuel, their cores collapse under their own gravity and trigger core-collapse supernovae. These violent disruptions leave behind dense neutron stars, black holes, or complete structural destruction.

The long span separating their explosions illustrates how slight differences in mass change how fast stars age. Even in a shared binary system, one star inevitably reaches its end before the other.

Why finding twin remnants matters to astrophysics

Astrophysicists have long predicted that massive binary stars should explode in stages separated by millennia. However, finding clear physical evidence of both explosions from a single system has proven extremely difficult.

The first star’s explosion usually blasts away gas and alters its neighbor, changing how the remaining star evolves over time. Finding both remnants intact allows researchers to study that secondary interaction up close for the first time. The result provides the first strong candidate example of a binary pair where both stars left observable supernova remnants behind. It gives scientists a practical reference point to test mathematical models of stellar evolution.

Where the science stands today

The research team uses the word “candidate” deliberately because certain historical details remain difficult to confirm. Scientists cannot directly observe the ancient orbit or prove that the two stars remained bound by gravity until their deaths.

Future telescope observations will measure the chemical composition and precise ages of both remnants to verify their shared origin. These additional details will help confirm whether both clouds truly share a single origin story.

Although these explosions occurred tens of thousands of years ago, the discovery has no practical effect on modern stargazing. Neither remnant is visible to the naked eye, but their shared history deepens our understanding of how giant stars end their lives.

Source: Miltiadis Michailidis et al., “Shared cloud interactions unveil a candidate binary-system supernova pair with no known analogue,” Nature Communications, July 21, 2026.
